stage_a.note: Uses enthusiastic language like freshest and most fun, highly energetic delivery.
Consistent high energy and clear passion when describing the product styles.
Friendly and approachable greeting, but mostly focused entirely on the pitch.

venture.description: Modern, patterned performance golf polo shirts targeting younger golfers.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Founder introduces himself, states the ask, and pitches the performance golf shirts designed to break boring golf culture.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: The panel members handle the sample shirts handed out by the founders.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Jokes about why anyone would play golf since he hates it, prompting a discussion on the demographic.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Laughs at the joke, then explains that golf has a boring history but is becoming popular with younger generations.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Points out that a customer does not actually need to play golf to wear the shirt.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Agrees but emphasizes they are technical performance shirts specifically designed for use on the golf course.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Compliments the product, noting that they are cool looking shirts regardless of the sport.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Challenges the uniqueness of the product, stating that there is a lot of similar stuff in the market.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Explains that several competing companies in golf have targeted the older golfer, leaving room for his brand.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Asks for the specific plan to gain market share and grow the brand.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Gives backstory of starting with twenty thousand dollars of his own money, hustling, and achieving seventy-two thousand in first year sales.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Praises his hustle and the initial sales figures, while another shark claps.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Continues his sales history, stating that in the second year he sold four hundred twelve thousand dollars.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Asks to confirm the four hundred twelve thousand dollar figure.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Confirms the figure and adds that year-to-date sales are seven hundred sixty thousand, projecting one point two million.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Expresses being impressed, calling him a hustler.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Explains that his sales have been entirely online until the last year.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Asks to confirm that the sales were all generated online.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Confirms and explains his model of dropping new polos, selling out quickly, and constantly reinvesting cash flow into inventory.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Asks if the customers wait specifically for the scheduled drop date to buy.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Confirms drops happen every two months, with particularly hot sellers moving into the core best sellers category.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Asks how many new product designs are released in a typical year.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: States thirty designs per season plus limited runs, and mentions building a team of ten graphic designers.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Asks for the manufacturing cost and the retail selling price of the shirts.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Sells for seventy-two dollars, cost dropped from forty to twenty-five, with overseas runs projecting fourteen.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Asks where the shirts are currently being manufactured.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Answers they are made in LA, and mentions starting wholesale with three hundred thousand committed for the next year.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Asks why the founder feels the need to expand into retail when online sales are doing so well.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: States that retail is an opportunity and it helps to grow the brand.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Asks how many shirts are produced in a typical production run.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: States that the runs will be one thousand to two thousand per shirt next year.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Praises the drop model as brilliant, noting it connects well with younger consumers trained by shoe drops.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Challenges that retail availability ruins the urgency of drops because nobody will wait in line for common inventory.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Concedes the point, saying he completely sees the difference.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Praises the incredible momentum and full margin cash flow the business has online right now.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Challenges the retail plan by stating that apparel brands often get buried and fail in retail.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Defends by stating that he only projects retail to be twenty-five percent or less of his total business.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Challenges that retail buyers will force price drops and ruin the margins, regardless of percentage.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Argues that if the competition is boring, the shirts will stand out and pop in a retail environment.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Agrees with Lori, suggesting that people gravitate to it and the brand can succeed in both channels.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Exits, stating that other sharks are more interested in a golf shirt investment and it is not right for her.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Offers three hundred thousand dollars for thirty percent equity, contingent on zero retail sales.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Argues that customers should have to beg to get the shirt on the drop date.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Disagrees with Kevin, stating that when a brand is hot it has to stay hot.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Expresses confusion over why the entire pitch became completely focused on the retail channel.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Says he is riding the wave right now and can pull back if it ever crashes.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Mentions a successful online clothing investment and states he likes how the business targets its customer.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Offers three hundred thousand dollars for twenty-five percent equity, promising not to forbid retail expansion.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Reiterates that the prospect of retail expansion always scares him.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Exits, advising the founder to just raise prices online instead of pursuing a retail strategy.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Exits, warning about the pressures and fees of retail real estate, not wanting to apply that pressure.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Prompts the founder to choose between the two standing offers.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Emphasizes his discipline and insistence on zero retail to protect the business.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Pitches himself over Kevin, asking the founder who he really wants wearing the shirt.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Counters Robert, asking if he would be willing to lower his equity requirement to twenty percent.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Declines the counter, insisting he needs at least twenty-five percent equity to partner.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Expresses hesitation that twenty-five percent is double what he was originally asking for.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Proposes a putting challenge to Robert for either twenty or twenty-five percent equity.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Accepts the putting challenge to finalize the deal terms.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Sets up the golf ball and prepares to take the putt.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Robert misses the putt, and the founder accepts the deal at twenty percent.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Jokes that he will bet five thousand dollars he can make the putt.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Jokes back that he will take another five percent if Kevin misses.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Takes the putt and misses it.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: The panel laughs at Kevin missing the putt.

decisions.note: Not the right investment for me, some other sharks are more interested.
Sales don't lie, but wants to forbid retail expansion to protect margins.
Likes the targeting of the customer, won't forbid selling in any channel.
Retail scares him, thinks the founder should just raise prices online instead.
Retail is about real estate and fees, doesn't want to put that pressure on the founder.
Asks Robert if he is willing to go down to 20 percent equity.

decisions.terms: 25% if Robert makes a putt, 20% if he misses.
decisions.note: Proposes a putting challenge to decide between 20 and 25 percent equity.

decisions.terms: Accepts the putting challenge for 20% or 25%.
decisions.note: Agrees to the founder's proposed putting challenge to determine the final equity.
Robert misses the putt, finalizing the deal at the lower equity stake.

record.notes: No major issues. The negotiation resolves via a physical putting challenge.
